extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers, and critics interested in the distinction and characteristics of literary vs genre fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the characteristics, cultural standing, and evaluative hallmarks used to identify and discuss literary fiction (as distinct from genre/commercial fiction). Useful for readers, students, critics, and writers learning what counts as 'literary' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven rather than plot-driven
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction "encompasses fiction that is more character-driven than plot-driven."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with genre fiction, where plot is the central concern. Evaluate whether a work foregrounds interiority, psychological depth, and character development over fast-moving plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of the human condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction often "examines the human condition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for themes of moral complexity, existential questioning, and sustained reflection on human experience rather than solely entertainment. Works that probe social, ethical, or personal dimensions fit this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considered serious art by critics
rubrics_metrics.description: A work is often labeled literary when it is "considered serious art by critics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment is frequently social/institutional: critics, academic-literary communities, and prestige outlets (e.g., The New York Review of Books, The New Yorker) influence the label. Inclusion in critical discussion or esteem is part of being 'literary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern with style and complexity of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction may be "more concerned with style and the complexity of the writing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge prose for craft: elegant, lyrical, layered, novel uses of language, structural experimentation, and attention to sentence-level artistry. Saricks' phrasing: "elegantly written, lyrical, and ... layered."

rubrics_metrics.name: Slower pace and allowance for digression
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction "may have a slower pace than popular fiction" and "allows itself to dawdle, to linger on stray beauties even at the risk of losing its way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate narrative tempo and tolerance for scenes or passages that prioritize atmosphere, detail, or reflection over forward plot propulsion. This can be a deliberate aesthetic choice rather than a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social commentary and political criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction may involve a concern with "social commentary, political criticism, or reflection on the human condition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a work engages consciously with social structures, politics, or critique of norms. Such engagement contributes to its literary evaluation when integrated with artistic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic focus on human character / 'non-genre' mainstream
rubrics_metrics.description: In one sense, literary fiction refers to "realistic fiction focused on human character, or more broadly, to 'all serious prose fiction outside the market genres'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a book is marketed and read as part of 'mainstream' literary discourse (realist, character-focused) rather than fitting a recognized marketing genre like mystery, romance, or SF. Note that 'mainstream' can mean either commercial bestseller mainstream or academic-literary mainstream—context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by prizes, canon, and institutions (literary merit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary merit is frequently signaled by awards and canonical acceptance (e.g., Nobel Prize in Literature, Booker Prize, inclusion in 'classic' lists or the Western canon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider institutional recognition (major prizes, scholarly attention, inclusion in lists like Modern Library/Penguin Classics) as evidence of perceived literary merit, while also noting debates and controversies about such selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classic status and enduring exemplary worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction includes "classic books, which are works ... that have been accepted as exemplary or noteworthy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess longevity, cultural impact, and continued critical regard when judging if a work approaches 'classic' status. Historical influence and repeated scholarly/educational use are indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-culture/aesthetic aspirations
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary fiction can be considered part of 'high culture' and associated with the aesthetic project of knowing "the best that has been said and thought in the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for engagement with philosophical, aesthetic, or moral ambitions; an orientation toward 'disinterested' cultural or intellectual refinement (as in Matthew Arnold's formulation) can mark a work as literary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap with genre elements does not preclude literary status
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works use elements of established genres (science fiction, crime, romance, historical fiction, magic realism) yet are still regarded as literary—e.g., Jane Austen's 'literary romance' or Margaret Atwood's speculative fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exclude works that deploy genre tropes; evaluate how those elements are used (e.g., to probe character, theme, or style) rather than dismissing them for being 'genre.' The slipstream and boundary-crossing works may be literary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between literary prestige and commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a noted contradiction in which "high sales figures are generally taken to mean the author has 'sold out'" and debates about marginalization of literary fiction versus popular genre success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, be aware of social biases that equate popularity with diminished literary value. Consider both critical reception and sales, but separate market success from artistic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and cultural shaping of the literary field
rubrics_metrics.description: The literary mainstream is shaped by early-20th-century fiction and the classic canon and is "dominated by the academic-literary community—university professors of literature; high-powered critics for prestige publications...and writers who take the first two groups seriously."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that judgments about what is 'literary' are historically and institutionally situated. Evaluate works with awareness of these shaping forces and possible exclusionary tendencies (e.g., canon formation).
